To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the myonuclear domain is not affected by training or age when fibers of similar size are analyzed, but is reduced in small fibers (<3,000 μm2) and increased in large fibers (>10,000 μm ^{2} ).
the relationship between fiber size, myonuclear content, and myonuclear domains is not affected by age, but is influenced by the proportion of small fibers in the muscle.
the relationship between myonuclear domain and fiber area is not affected by age or training status.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between skeletal fiber area and myo-nuclei content and how this relationship changes with age.
how the muscle fibers are affected by aging.
the regulation of skeletal muscle fiber size.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

fiber size and age have no direct effect on the myonuclear domain but that fiber size and the age‐related increase in the proportion of smaller fibers may be responsible for the observed reduction in myonuclear domains in the old subjects.
there is a relationship between fiber size, myonuclear content, and myonuclear area (domain) in human skeletal muscle.
the relationship between fiber size, myonuclear content and domain is complex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fiber size matters for myonuclear content, but not for myonuclear domains.
the myonuclear domains are larger in fibers that are >3,000 um2.
we have shown that the myonuclear domain is not a fixed value, and that the domain is dependent on the fiber size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fiber size matters more than age.
the relationship between fiber size (area) and myonuclear number is linear.
